post1.text:
Hiring senior executives is not a growth strategy. It is a delay tactic disguised as one.

Companies scaling past $50M often assume that adding experienced leaders to the org chart will solve the complexity that comes with rapid growth. Stanford researchers studying AI adoption across organizations found something that applies far beyond technology: executives frequently lack the internal clarity needed to lead new initiatives before they deploy them. The same is true for scaling broadly.

Here is what actually matters at that stage:

1. Your current leaders need to grow faster than the business does. If they cannot, new hires inherit a broken system.

2. Leadership capacity is a bottleneck before capital ever is. Most $50M companies have enough money. They do not have enough leaders who can think at $200M.

3. Culture does not scale on its own. Someone has to actively carry it upward through every new layer of the organization.

Before your next executive search, ask yourself this: are you building leaders or just buying them?

#LeadershipDevelopment #ScalingBusiness #ExecutiveLeadership

post2.text:
A recent piece from Stanford Graduate School of Business makes a sharp point: most executives do not fully understand what they are scaling before they scale it. The context was AI, but the lesson hits every growth-stage company.

At Autobahn, we see this pattern constantly with companies moving from $50M toward $500M. Leaders rush to scale systems, teams, and technology before they have diagnosed what is actually working. The result is that they grow the wrong things faster.

The companies that scale well do one thing differently: their leadership team builds understanding before building infrastructure. That discipline separates the companies that double revenue from the ones that double their problems.

If your leadership team is preparing to scale something significant in 2025, read this first: https://news.google.com/rss/articles/CBMirwFBVV95cUxOYVhzWHYzT1VheXhTVGVNSHgtQlFMMHFPZHFoUmxYQTJ2SllrZG91d2trSW1UTHdBdmlhNVB6Q2FZeDVUSnRkWm1qaFRaN3ZDR2JvXzdtbkkwVF9rbXBwZ3QtWFp3ME92aXVESVRrY1RVUF9HWnp0ZUNJYktpN180aGx2OURxdm4wc0Z6UU1CeFdhVTFrLTloQ05wLWgwVThrNjZkZXBIMWNHcUkzc2tv

post3.text:
Strive Health recently expanded its executive team specifically to support its next phase of scale. Smart move. But adding leadership talent is only half the equation.

Chapter 1 of Rock Your Business, titled Lead Like Lives Depend On It, written by Katherine Slain, takes on the harder half. Katherine makes the case that leadership at the $50M to $500M stage is not just a professional responsibility. It carries the weight of every employee, family, and stakeholder connected to your organization.

The leaders who scale companies successfully are not simply more experienced. They operate with a different standard of accountability, one that most leadership books never actually demand of you.

Katherine's chapter sets that tone from page one, and it does not let up.

post1.text:
Most business owners spend decades building a company and about six months thinking about how to exit it. That imbalance is expensive.

A recent Entrepreneur piece made this point plainly: founders obsess over growth metrics but treat exit planning as something to handle later. Later almost always costs them money.

Here is what leaders running $50M+ businesses need to understand:

1. Your multiple is not determined at the time of sale. It is built over years through recurring revenue, clean financials, and management depth that does not depend on the founder.

2. Buyers pay a premium for predictability, not just profit. EBITDA matters, but so does how repeatable your revenue is.

3. The gap between what you think your company is worth and what the market will pay is almost always larger than you expect. Closing that gap takes time you may not have if you wait.

If you sold your business today, would the buyer see what you see when you look at it?

post2.text:
A recent piece from Forbes on exit planning lays out a solid framework for business owners thinking about their eventual transition. It covers the basics well: financial readiness, legal structure, and timing.

What it does not cover is the work that happens before any of that matters for companies in the $50M to $500M range.

At that scale, the real leverage is in how you maximize your multiple before you ever enter a process. That means building a management team that runs without you, documenting what makes your revenue durable, and understanding how a strategic buyer will value you differently than a financial one.

Exit planning is not an event. It is a discipline. The earlier you treat it that way, the better the outcome.

Read the Forbes piece here and then ask yourself whether your business is actually ready: https://news.google.com/rss/articles/CBMiogFBVV95cUxPQjFIYXhibGVtZGsyVmtwMGZpTjdobTVlcEJOMURid0JybUZzRjlzc212dU85c29LdEFYMXJDRU1vNzYtVXZIZzFhZVU4T3RpdzZ5VnR2bkZ2ZXJPRG83d1hiTFJ4UF85WHR5QnNJc0wzdEdqS0xsQXdFVi1JeG0zSGxYY3ZtX1ZUYkxWaDRpcE9sTENEVlNuN1pKTkxzZmRyOGc

post3.text:
J.P. Morgan Private Bank recently published a breakdown of business exit strategies that is worth reading. It is thorough. What it cannot do is tell you how to engineer a higher multiple before you get to that point.

That is exactly what Chapter 2 of Rock Your Business does.

The chapter, titled Maximize Your Multiple to Achieve Your Exit, was written by Paul Belair and George Hohman. They work with companies in the $50M to $500M range and have seen firsthand what separates a good exit from a great one. One of their core ideas: the actions that move your multiple are not taken during a sale process. They are taken two to five years before it starts.

There is a specific set of value drivers they lay out that most owners overlook entirely. We will share more as the release gets closer.

post1.text:
Most strategic plans fail not because of bad strategy, but because execution is treated as an afterthought.

Companies at the $50M mark often have decent plans sitting in decks that nobody references after Q1. The gap between strategy and daily action is where growth goes to die.

Wrike's recent move into strategic portfolio management signals something the market already knows: organizations are desperate for tools that connect boardroom decisions to ground-level work. That gap is real, and it is expensive.

Here is what scaling leaders need to understand:

1. Strategy without a cadence is a wish list. Weekly operational rhythms tied to annual goals are non-negotiable.

2. The team executing the plan must help build it. Buy-in is not a soft concept. It is a performance variable.

3. Faster results require fewer priorities, not more. Organizations that chase ten initiatives rarely nail one.

If your leadership team cannot recite your top three priorities without looking at a slide deck, what does that tell you about your execution engine?

post2.text:
A recent piece in HousingWire highlights how NAR is revisiting its strategic plan with a sharper focus on speed and accountability. Leadership is pushing for faster, more measurable results rather than long runway timelines.

This matters for every company scaling past $50M.

At Autobahn, we see it constantly: leadership teams spend months building beautiful strategic plans, then struggle to hold anyone accountable to them. The fix is not a better plan. It is a tighter execution system with shorter feedback loops and clear ownership at every level.

Speed of execution separates companies that reach $500M from those that stall out at $100M. If your strategy review happens once a year, you are already behind.

Read the full NAR piece and ask yourself: how often is your team actually measuring against the plan?

When NAR leadership pushed to accelerate results from their strategic plan, they were wrestling with the same tension that Rafa Loyo and Jim Randall unpack in Chapter 3 of our upcoming book, Rock Your Business.

The chapter is called "What We Learned Selling Fish Food and Nike Shoes," and the title alone should tell you it is not your typical strategy content.

Rafa and Jim draw on real business experience across wildly different industries to show how a strong execution framework has to be built from the ground up, not handed down from a whiteboard session. One insight that stands out: the business you are running today may not be the right vehicle for the strategy you are trying to execute. That distinction changes everything.

post1.text:
Most companies at $50M don't have a sales strategy. They have a sales habit.

There's a difference. A habit is what your team does by default. A strategy is what you choose to do on purpose. And according to recent research from Bain, the B2B companies that repeatedly win new customers aren't doing more activity. They're doing fewer things with far more precision.

Here's what that looks like in practice for scaling companies:

1. Your best customers share a profile. If you can't describe that profile in two sentences, you're selling to anyone and hoping.

2. Repeatability beats heroics. One superstar rep is a liability. A documented process that average reps can execute is a growth engine.

3. Revenue targets without a customer acquisition model are just wishful thinking. The math has to work before the quarter starts.

Companies between $50M and $500M bleed the most revenue not from bad products, but from undisciplined go-to-market motion.

So here's the question: If your top salesperson left tomorrow, would your pipeline survive?

post2.text:
A recent piece from Bain on B2B growth lays out something we see constantly with scaling companies: the firms that reliably capture new customers aren't guessing. They have a repeatable formula.

Most $50M to $500M businesses treat customer acquisition like an art form. A few great reps, strong relationships, and good timing. That works until it doesn't.

At Autobahn, we see the ceiling this creates every time. Growth stalls not because the market dried up, but because there's no system underneath the salespeople.

If your revenue growth depends on individuals rather than process, you don't have a sales strategy. You have a dependency.

Read the Bain piece and ask yourself where your team lands on that spectrum.

post1.text:
Your brand is not your logo. It is not your tagline. It is the feeling someone gets the moment they interact with your company, and most $50M+ businesses have never intentionally designed that feeling.

Campari's approach to brand management proves this point. Rather than letting heritage become a liability, they actively shape how their brands connect with culture at each stage of growth. The lesson is not about being trendy. It is about being deliberate.

Here is what scaling companies consistently get wrong about branding:

1. They treat it as a marketing department problem, not a leadership priority.
2. They confuse brand awareness with brand clarity. People knowing your name means nothing if they cannot articulate what you stand for.
3. They let brand identity drift during rapid growth, which is exactly when consistency matters most.

A $100M company with a blurry brand identity will struggle to reach $500M. The market does not reward ambiguity.

What does your brand actually feel like to a first-time customer?

post2.text:
A recent piece in Marketing Dive highlights how Ulta's CMO thinks about blending brand building with omnichannel marketing, and it surfaces something that most mid-market leaders overlook entirely.

At scale, brand and channel strategy cannot live in separate rooms. The companies that reach $500M are not just executing on more channels. They are ensuring the brand experience is coherent across every single touchpoint, whether that is a retail shelf, a mobile app, or a customer service call.

For companies in the $50M to $500M range, this is where significant revenue gets left on the table. Inconsistent brand experience quietly erodes trust, and eroded trust slows growth.

If your marketing team and your operations team are not in regular conversation about brand experience, that is a gap worth closing now.

Read the full piece here: https://news.google.com/rss/articles/CBMiogFBVV95cUxPRlFnSEozTXJJdnl5aWFJQTFGR0tkcnhrUnUyOTNZNlIwcHZiLWFnbm0tQ0FWZEZCTWZvdUFQeEFvQkIwOHdpMmZBR3I5WmNjRmFYb0xJMGhQWmJHYUdWUVdyWndOWTYwR1ZQQ2E4V1dMV2NrT0hpRzNaU1VKdUdoZHMwSFB4SlhYTkZKZ2hDdEdsSkJ6TW91UTZTWlNGaGVmcUE

post3.text:
The conversation around Ulta's omnichannel branding strategy connects directly to something our upcoming book tackles head on.

Chapter 5 of Rock Your Business, titled "What Does Your Marketing Smell Like?", was authored by Kayli Simpson and Yasmin West, and it asks a question most executives have never seriously considered: if your brand had a scent, would your customers recognize it in the dark?

That is not a gimmick. It is a framework for evaluating whether your brand identity is truly sensory and consistent, or just a document sitting in a folder somewhere.

Simpson and West lay out a practical approach for growth-stage companies to audit and sharpen their brand presence before scaling costs amplify every inconsistency.

The insight that sticks: the brands that scale cleanly are the ones that got intentional about identity before they needed to, not after.

Rock Your Business, available soon. Follow us for updates.

post1.text:
Hiring more people is not a growth strategy. It is a cost strategy.

Most companies scaling past $50M default to volume when they feel the pressure of growth. More recruiters. More job postings. More headcount. But SHRM's latest research on hiring trends makes a strong case that the companies winning right now are doing the opposite: they are hiring fewer people with far greater intentionality.

Here is what that looks like in practice for leaders running $50M to $500M businesses:

First, role clarity before recruitment. If you cannot define what success looks like in the seat after 90 days, you are not ready to hire.

Second, your hiring process is a signal. Slow, disorganized, or inconsistent processes tell top candidates exactly how you run your business.

Third, culture fit is not a vibe. It is a set of definable behaviors that you either screen for or you do not.

Growth companies that treat talent with precision rather than volume consistently outperform those that treat headcount as a solution.

So here is the question: Is your next hire solving a real problem, or just making a problem feel smaller?

post2.text:
A recent piece in SHRM breaks down what they are calling the new rules of hiring in 2026, and the core argument is worth paying attention to: precision in hiring is now outperforming scale.

For companies in the $50M to $500M growth range, this is not a trend to watch. It is a decision to make right now.

At Autobahn, we see this pattern constantly. Scaling companies that invest in defining the right role before opening the requisition save months of drag and avoid costly mis-hires that stall momentum.

The leaders getting this right are treating talent acquisition as a strategic function, not an HR function. That shift in ownership changes everything.

If your hiring process is not producing the people your growth plan requires, the process is the problem.

Read the full SHRM piece here: https://news.google.com/rss/articles/CBMioAFBVV95cUxPRFVYR0VscXJpMmVqV2dwazJDTkstVDJTNG9uTlZlWHJPVkFqQ0MzZTRQSUYwUDZweWw2dE52THZKSnhBTzQtb1g5UUYzbmJTbjFJcXlVYno2ZzU4aE0yNVRwN2RIN05xTWJVWnZQejVyY2xRNmJ2SF83QmVHel9GYmdWTEdEMWZLMVk5OThMNTF0TmdKR1F4bG84cnZRZ0FU?oc=5

post1.text:
More KPIs will not save your business. They might actually be killing it.

Oracle NetSuite recently outlined 30 financial metrics companies should track heading into 2026. Thirty. For most leadership teams, that list does not clarify performance. It creates noise that buries the two or three numbers that actually drive decisions.

Here is what scaling companies need to understand:

1. Tracking more metrics is often a substitute for making hard choices. If everything is a priority, nothing is.

2. The metrics that matter at $50M are not the same ones that matter at $150M. Your KPI stack should evolve with your business model, not stay frozen at whatever your first CFO set up.

3. A leadership team that cannot recite its top five metrics from memory has too many metrics. Full stop.

The companies we see stall between $50M and $500M are rarely short on data. They are short on clarity about which data changes behavior.

What is the one number your entire leadership team is actually held accountable to right now?

post2.text:
A recent piece in CLA Connect breaks down the KPIs manufacturers should use to improve company performance. It is a solid operational rundown, and for manufacturers pushing past $50M, it is worth a read.

But here is what the article does not address: knowing which KPIs to track is only half the problem. The harder challenge is building the organizational discipline to act on them consistently, especially when growth is accelerating and leadership bandwidth is stretched thin.

At Autobahn, we work with scaling companies every day who have dashboards full of the right metrics and cultures that still ignore them when things get uncomfortable.

Data without accountability is decoration.

If you are in manufacturing and trying to tighten your performance management as you scale, start here: https://news.google.com/rss/articles/CBMiugFBVV95cUxNc3hGVVVxVnMwVEpLcmxaNWJzaURJbERjczZaSDhlcnhvOFlHX1VZU0tETkctQjFqRVhZVkNtcFNoUWtfSmRhSmU5N3pYc25IVzlfTEs5TjFZWk1RTmhZd2JzSkpPSXVmQndRRHRBM29CaDBoWnVWRXcxMnBhWkcwT3dmWTAwSDFSeS1hYzFtRUNtd05nWE9PX25nbzRfc2ZzSjVFVURMY0hMRkdVMmtOdjVOYUluUXJIcEE

post3.text:
Most leadership teams at $50M-plus companies are not lacking metrics. They are drowning in them.

Chapter 7 of our upcoming book, Rock Your Business, is called Death by KPIs for a reason. Authors Hector Arias, Matt Radicelli, and Jim Randall have worked inside scaling companies long enough to know that an overloaded scorecard does not drive performance. It diffuses responsibility and gives everyone a reason to point at a different number when results disappoint.

One insight they share: the most dangerous KPIs are not the wrong ones. They are the right ones that no single person owns. Accountability without clarity is just measurement theater.

If your leadership team is tracking dozens of metrics but still arguing about what the real priorities are, this chapter was written for you.

Rock Your Business, available soon. Follow us for updates.

posts.blog_hook: Most scaling companies do not have a data problem. They have a discipline problem. Leadership teams between $50M and $500M are routinely buried under dashboards packed with metrics that no one fully owns and few actually act on. The companies that break through are not tracking more. They are tracking less, with ruthless clarity about which numbers change behavior and who is accountable when they move in the wrong direction.

post1.text:
AI is not a productivity tool. It is a decision-making environment. And most executives have not figured that out yet.

A recent Fortune report found that nine out of ten executives say AI has not moved the needle on productivity. That number should stop you cold. Companies are spending real money on AI tools and seeing nothing back.

Here is what scaling companies need to understand:

1. Adoption without architecture fails. Dropping AI into existing workflows does not fix broken workflows. It accelerates them.

2. The productivity gap is a measurement gap. Most leaders are not tracking the right outputs. They are counting hours, not decisions.

3. Your third screen matters more than your first two. Where AI sits in your team's daily environment determines whether it changes behavior or just adds noise.

Companies between $50M and $500M are in the most dangerous position. Large enough to waste serious resources on AI. Small enough that those mistakes are not recoverable.

So here is the real question: Is your team using AI, or is AI changing how your team thinks?

post2.text:
A recent piece in Fortune reported that 90% of executives say AI has not improved productivity, yet companies are still cutting jobs in anticipation of AI doing more work.

That gap is a serious problem for scaling companies.

At Autobahn, we see this pattern constantly. Leaders buy the promise of AI before they build the process around it. The tool arrives. The workflow does not change. The results disappoint. And now you have fewer people and slower output.

If you are running a company between $50M and $500M, AI integration is not an IT decision. It is an operational strategy decision. Get that wrong and you are not just behind on technology. You are behind on growth.

Read the full article and then ask yourself whether your AI rollout has a real productivity plan behind it.

Nine out of ten executives say AI has not improved productivity. That finding from Fortune does not surprise Hudson Shank and Jonathan Slain one bit.

In Chapter 8 of Rock Your Business, titled The Third Monitor Theory, Hudson and Jonathan lay out exactly why most AI adoption stalls before it delivers. The issue is not the technology. It is where and how AI enters a leader's actual working environment.

The Third Monitor Theory offers a specific, physical framework for how executives at scaling companies should position AI as a genuine decision-making layer, not a bolt-on feature nobody uses by lunch.

If your company is growing past $50M and you have spent real money on AI tools that have not changed how your leadership team operates, this chapter was written for you.

post1.text:
The leaders most likely to destroy their companies are the ones who never doubt themselves.

Imposter syndrome gets treated like a flaw to fix. It is not. For executives scaling companies past $50M, that persistent internal friction is often the last honest signal you are getting about where the business actually stands.

Forbes recently reported that imposter syndrome follows high achievers all the way to the top. That tracks. But the real insight is not that it follows them. It is that the leaders who learn to use it rather than suppress it make better decisions under pressure.

Three things scaling leaders should know:

1. Self-doubt at this level is data, not weakness. It points to capability gaps before your org chart does.

2. The instinct to project certainty to your team often creates the exact blind spots that slow growth.

3. Leaders who normalize their own uncertainty build teams that surface problems faster.

The question is not how to get rid of the doubt. It is whether you have built a culture where that doubt drives better thinking instead of better performance.

What do you do with the moments when you genuinely are not sure you are the right person for the next stage of growth?

post2.text:
A recent piece in Fast Company argues we should stop calling it imposter syndrome altogether. The label, they suggest, misplaces the problem on the individual rather than on systems and environments that breed self-doubt.

That reframe matters more than it sounds, especially for companies scaling past $50M.

At that stage, leadership identity is in constant flux. Founders and executives are being asked to operate in roles they have never held before, often without a clear model to follow. When self-doubt shows up, blaming personal psychology is the easiest answer. It is rarely the right one.

At Autobahn, we see this consistently. The doubt is real, but the source is usually structural. New complexity, faster decisions, thinner margins for error.

Before you pathologize the feeling, examine the environment producing it.

Read the full piece here: https://news.google.com/rss/articles/CBMidkFVX3lxTE9PRnBrU1NWWm1BeEl3dk5qVjFRc0M0T2ctZW9fbjdWd2NmdFlUZVVNeW9JV0VTWkktVmp0MlVjbFVEMXEweWZBS1d6bFBSMVNoNFVfWm5WaFo0aG1PT1RJN0p2Ylc0SkRONnBBcDYzZmNEUUJsRFE

post3.text:
How could you be this successful and still feel like you have no idea what you are doing?

That question sits at the center of Chapter 9 in our upcoming book, Rock Your Business: Navigating the Road from $50 Million to $500 Million and Beyond. The chapter, titled "How Could You Be Successful and Not Have It?", was authored by Samantha Frost, Caleb Hawkins, and Rafa Loyo.

Their work goes beyond naming the feeling. They identify a specific pattern in leaders at the growth stage where past success becomes a psychological liability. The skills that got you to $50M can quietly convince you that you should already know how to get to $500M.

You do not. And that is not a problem. It is a starting point.

Chapter 9 gives leaders a way to work with that tension rather than hide from it.

Rock Your Business, available soon. Follow us for updates.

What most of them do not know is that feeling is not a warning sign about their fitness to lead. It is a predictable feature of genuine growth. Here is what to do with it.

post1.text:
Most founders treat their personal life like a leftover agenda item. Business strategy gets the whiteboard. Life gets whatever is left.

That is a dangerous operating model.

A recent Entrepreneur piece drives this home: founders obsess over growth plans but rarely build an intentional plan for what comes after. The exit, the transition, the identity shift. It blindsides them.

Here is what leaders scaling past $50M should understand:

1. Your business plan and your life plan are not separate documents. They should be built in parallel, with equal rigor.

2. The skills that got you to $50M often work against the life you say you want at $500M. Speed, control, and urgency become liabilities outside the office.

3. Designing your work around your life is not a luxury. For leaders at this scale, it is a retention strategy, a succession strategy, and a personal sustainability strategy all at once.

The companies that scale best are usually led by founders who have answered a harder question first.

What does the life you are building this business toward actually look like?

post2.text:
A recent piece in Fortune, produced with Morgan Stanley, lays out a roadmap for entrepreneurs navigating life after a business sale. It covers identity, finances, purpose, and the psychological weight of the transition.

At Autobahn, we see this challenge start much earlier than the exit. Leaders scaling from $50M to $500M are already losing themselves inside their companies. By the time a sale happens, many have no idea who they are outside of the business.

The smarter move is building a life plan before you need one. Not after the wire clears.

If you lead a scaling company and have not had a serious conversation about what you want your life to look like in five years, start there.

Read the Fortune piece here: https://news.google.com/rss/articles/CBMiiwFBVV95cUxPdnZpWG94aDF5el9jOUtxNWhVYlFXZ3FKejZHQkJEOTVVSmN2VE1COEtTb3lkTnJ1VENGTVoxWGUzOHhYdlJ4QUV6bW9IajBVTEQ2cm5vUWRST3pCcWlxXzNzNHNMQlRmSURudzZZbFNuWkx2YUZWakN5ME1mcVU0Rm9XcFdMOXQzNFo4

post3.text:
Fortune and Morgan Stanley just published a roadmap for entrepreneurs after a business sale. It is a good resource. But the leaders who need it most are often the ones who never saw it coming.

Chapter 10 of our upcoming book, Rock Your Business, addresses this directly. The chapter is called Coming Up for Air, written by Samantha Frost alongside Jonathan and Katherine Slain.

The core idea: scaling a business is not just a financial journey. It is a personal one. And if you do not build a deliberate life plan alongside your growth strategy, the company will fill every inch of space you leave open.

Chapter 10 gives scaling leaders a framework for designing work and life on their own terms, before the business makes those decisions for them.
